newsitem.title: UK: Gilts hit as rate pressure persists after budget.
newsitem.headline: Gilts hit as rate pressure persists after budget.

text.p: UK gilts surrendered early gains and reversed into negative territory as the fiscal tightening in Wednesday's British budget failed to take pressure off interest rate rises, analysts said.
Chancellor Gordon Brown announced 5.5 billion sterling worth of fiscal tightening for 1997/97, 1.5 billion more than the market had forecast.

"Strip out the windfall tax, which he said was included in the 5.5 billion stg figure, and tightening will be 2-3 billion, which really isn't enough. And that really does point to higher interest rates ahead," said Mark Wall, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
September gilt futures on LIFFE raced to a fresh contract high of 105-05 minutes after Brown started to deliver the Labour government's first budget. But profit taking soon set in.
By 1615 GMT, the September gilt contract had shed 22/32 on the day to 113-30, compared to 114-30 just before the budget.
Analysts said prospects for the gilt market were dimmed by the budget's failure to cool down the scorching consumer spending, leaving monetary policy to take up the slack.
"I will still be looking for a rate rise probably in August, possibly in July," said Mark Ramsden, economist at Stone and McCarthy Res Associates.

One bright spot for gilts was Brown's forecast of public sector borrowing requirement which came in at a lower-than-expected 13.25 billion sterling for 1997/98, from 23 billion in 1996/97. Analysts had expected the PSBR of around 16 billion.
A five-year deficit reduction plan based on the government's "golden rule" of only borrowing to finance investment -- around one percent of GDP -- was also viewed positively.
But the good news was offset by a lack of tough measures to rein back consumption, and stronger emphasis instead on the corporate sector, analysts said.

"A lot of it focused on the corporate side and the market after recent data had built in quite a strong expectation that he was going to do more to slow down the pace of consumption," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.
The yield curve steepened after the budget as analysts reassessed interest rate forecasts before the BOE's monetary policy meeting on July 9 and 10.
"We are going to steepen a bit now because flattening was coming not only from expectations of rate hike but also from the performance of long term gilts," said Rayner.
But any further steepening would likely be mild. "The curve has still got to flatten once the Bank of England starts hiking rates again," Rayner said.
The spread between yields on two-year and 25-year gilts stood at 22 basis points after the budget, some three basis points wider.
"It's a disappointing budget really...he really looks as if he's decided...to leave it to the Bank of England," Rayner said.
The short sterling strip also eased on interest rate concerns after Brown forecast consumer spending up by 4.5 percent this year and 4.0 percent in 1998.
The December short sterling future contract was now discounting official rates of around 7.25 percent by the end of the year, from their current 6.5 percent.
